title: Medicine in the Islamic World
objective: After this level you can describe the work of Ibn Sina and the hospitals of Baghdad and Cairo.
summary: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, translated into Latin in the 12th century, was a European textbook until the mid-1600s. Bimaristans admitted all; Qalawun's hospital was free.

cards.headline: Europe’s doctors were still learning from a Persian’s textbook in the 1600s.
cards.body: It was written in Arabic, far from any European classroom. How did it get onto their reading lists? And what did hospitals look like where it was written?

cards.headline: The boy who found medicine easy
cards.body: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara in 980 and died in Hamadan in 1037. He turned to medicine at 16 and, by his own account, found it “easy”. (Most of us found algebra hard at 16.) His great work, the Canon of Medicine, runs to five books, from general principles and simple drugs to diseases and compound remedies.

cards.headline: Europe’s textbook
cards.body: In the 12th century Gerard of Cremona translated the Canon into Latin. Between 1500 and 1674 some sixty editions were published in Europe, mostly for university medical training, and it served as a textbook there until the mid-17th century. Imagine a course reading list that stays the same for centuries.
cards.callout: Written in Arabic, taught in Latin

cards.headline: Hospitals for everyone
cards.body: The Islamic world built hospitals called bimaristans, a Persian word meaning “location of disease”. Harun al-Rashid founded one in Baghdad, and al-Ma’mun founded more. Hospitals at Baghdad, Damascus and Córdoba admitted patients regardless of religion, race or social rank. In Cairo, Sultan Qalawun’s hospital of 1284–85 treated rich and poor free of charge, with separate wards for different illnesses. No insurance card required.

Bimaristans treated patients of every faith and rank

questions.prompt: Until roughly when did Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine serve as a textbook in Europe?

options.label: The 20th century
options.rationale: Too late: it faded by the mid-1600s.

questions.explanation: The Canon served as a medical textbook in Europe until the mid-17th century.

questions.prompt: What set the hospitals of Baghdad, Damascus and Córdoba apart?

options.label: They treated only the caliph’s soldiers
options.rationale: They were open far more widely.

They charged patients by their religion

questions.explanation: These hospitals admitted patients regardless of religious belief, race or social order.

questions.prompt: Level 37’s Sphere was a university astronomy textbook. What did Europe’s universities mostly use Ibn Sina’s Canon for?

options.label: Teaching canon law
options.rationale: Despite its name, the Canon was a medical book.
